title: ChatGPT Ads: Are they worth it or just a dud- here’s what the data says
summary: ChatGPT ads are open to every store now. Here's what clicks really cost, why your product feed matters more than your budget, and who should sit this out.
body_markdown:
The hype dust has finally settled and the saloon doors have stopped swinging. There’s a new gunslinger in town: ChatGPT ads.


Google, Meta and Amazon have spent decades perfecting the art of getting brands in front of buyers. Now ChatGPT has walked into the same dusty street, except its customers are a bit torn about whether it would fire duds or really be counted among legends.


In most internet townhalls, the general spirit is more inclined towards the former than the latter. A while back, someone on r/ChatGPT[tried to explain why the whole idea bothered them](https://www.reddit.com/r/ChatGPT/comments/1tk9pvz/chatgpt_is_about_to_show_you_ads_and_honestly_i/) .


> *“...I use chatgpt daily for work. the idea of it recommending a tool mid-conversation and getting paid for it makes me uncomfortable in a way I'm still figuring out. Like it's not just an ad. it's an ad dressed up as advice from something you trust.”*


That discomfort isn't exactly hard to understand. When you’re used to asking ChatGPT for an answer, an ad inside that answer can feel less like a billboard and more like your trusted bartender suddenly getting a commission for recommending a specific kind of whiskey. Even a survey[found 63% of adults](https://www.emarketer.com/content/faq-on-chatgpt-advertising--formats--costs--early-strategies-win) saying ads in AI search results would make them trust the output less.


But the ads have shipped anyway and now they have gone from a $200,000-minimum experiment to something you can switch on this afternoon with a card and a product feed. The[clicks are reportedly running roughly $3 to $5](https://www.indexlab.ai/guides/chatgpt-ads/costs) , which is not exotic money for anyone already buying Google ads.


So, the questions that you must be finding yourself asking would be: Do ChatGPT ads work? Are they worth it for a store your size? Truth is nobody is going to give you a straight answer- neither the guy selling you a course on AI advertising nor the influencer announcing yet another AI revolution , so let me share some data backed research with you.


Let’s look at what the ChatGPT ads costs, who actually sees it, how it compares with other channels, and whether there's sufficient reason for you to pull the trigger.


## What changed since January


In two simple words: a lot!


If you read a hot take on ChatGPT ads in January and thought that you’ll get back to it later, almost everything about it has since expired.


- That $200,000 minimum spend is now gone. The[self-serve Ads Manager](https://topgrowthmarketing.com/how-much-do-chatgpt-ads-cost/) opened to all US businesses on May 5, 2026, and there is no floor now beyond a card on file.


- The other big complaint was that advertisers were flying blind, paying premium rates for impression counts and nothing else. That's largely fixed too. OpenAI now[gives you a tracking pixel](https://developers.openai.com/ads/conversion-tracking) , a server-side Conversions API, and a click identifier called oppref that matches the sale back to the ad that caused it.


- In September 2026,[conversion-based bidding became generally available](https://www.indexlab.ai/guides/chatgpt-ads/costs) , which means you can tell the system to chase purchases instead of clicks. OpenAI's own early benchmark claims a median 44% lower cost per result, though that came from a sample of 27 advertisers, so treat it as a optimistic signal rather than the word of law carved on a stone tablet.


- Lastly, since September 4, 2026,[shopping results inside ChatGPT](https://www.surebright.com/blog/openais-instant-checkout-fell-short--walmart-does-this-end-the-ai-ecommerce-revolution) are exclusive to brands with a connected product feed, and the platform opened in more than 30 new countries the same week.


But the biggest change OpenAI has seen is in its CEO, Sam Altman’s outlook towards advertisements. The guy went from hating “ads as an aesthetic choice” to finding it “cool things to do that actually seem helpful to users”[in a single year](https://searchengineland.com/sam-altman-chatgpt-ads-pivot-463150) . I guess people do evolve (especially when their analysts show them[a forecast of billion dollars in new revenue](https://searchengineland.com/chatgpt-with-ads-coming-454590) from a thing they hate or tell them[how users are dropping off in droves](https://www.surebright.com/blog/are-merchants-done-with-chatgpt-for-good-heres-what-the-numbers-say) .)


That leads us to a very interesting question... why hasn’t any other AI tool done this yet?


### Why Anthropic and Perplexity refuse to ride into this town


Perplexity did ride the town on an ‘AI search advertising first’ pony - testing sponsored follow-up questions from late 2024. Then it stopped taking new advertisers in October 2025 and[walked away completely in February 2026](https://searchengineland.com/perplexity-stops-testing-advertising-469452) . One wonders what they found staring in the abyss.


The reason wasn't money, because ads were barely a rounding error for them at[roughly $20,000 out of $34 million in 2024 revenue](https://influencermarketinghub.com/advertising-perplexity-growing-ad-platform/) . A[Perplexity executive said](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/880562/perplexity-ditches-ai-ads) that the trouble with ads is that users simply start doubting everything.


Anthropic went further,[publishing an essay in February 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-is-a-space-to-think) committing to keep Claude ad-free permanently, arguing that sponsored placements would conflict with what the assistant is for. Will that stay that way or change after a year like Sam Altman’s outlook... only time can tell. For now, their vision of a trillion-dollar IPO is keeping them growing massively even as OpenAI has been struggling. The company has a far larger free population to pay for.


So the split says less about ethics than about who needs the ad revenue. However, the practical consequence for you is the same either way: a meaningful chunk of AI search traffic has no paid slots to buy at all. On those surfaces, showing up is earned or lost.


## Let’s start by understanding who’s on the other side of your impression?


Ads only show on ChatGPT's free and Go tiers.


Everyone on Plus, Pro, Enterprise or Education sees nothing. As of July 2026,[51% of US free-tier replies carried a sponsored block](https://tech-insider.org/chatgpt-ads-rollout-2026/) , so the inventory is dense where it exists and completely absent where it doesn't.


How the ad looks like inside the chat


That creates an awkward pattern. An agency[ran a test in June 2026](https://choice.marketing/blog/chatgpt-ads-2026-field-guide/) and got 8,940 impressions and 58 clicks at a 0.65% click-through rate, with no signups to show for it. Their diagnosis was an equal combination of uncomfortable and honest: the more closely someone matched their ideal customer, the likelier that person was already paying for an ad-free plan.


**For B2B sellers** , that ceiling is a nightmare on ChatGPT ads. The operations director evaluating your software probably has the money to afford a Plus subscription. But whether they use that or stay on Claude isn’t a clearly answerable question.


**For DTC and retail** , this matters less. Most consumer shoppers are on the free tier, and those are exactly the people likely to see these ads while asking for gift ideas, comparing mattresses, or deciding what to buy.


That might sound like a mixed bag. Let’s take a closer look.


## Comparing the good, the bad, and the ugly of ChatGPT Ads


Let’s start with the good parts-


- Campaign setup takes minutes rather than an afternoon.


- Targeting uses something called context hints, which are plain-language descriptions of the conversations you want to appear in, so instead of guessing the intent behind certain keywords, you describe the problem your customer is trying to solve.


- Ads appear after the user has received an answer, meaning that person has already explained their situation in far more detail than any search box would capture.


Now the rough parts -


- It is more expensive than other platforms. When[one agency tested it](https://eyekiller.com/blog/chatgpt-ads-our-honest-verdict) , their CPM ran around $21.20 against Meta's typical $9.24 to $13.86, and their cost per click hit $2.69 versus around $2 on Google Search. Though some US advertisers, at the time of writing this, are seeing[roughly $3 to $5 per click](https://www.indexlab.ai/guides/chatgpt-ads/costs) .


- Traffic quality lags too, with engagement time per session initially running at half of what Google Ads delivered, though there can be workarounds for that like tightening your context hints and targeting only one country.


- Reporting is thin. There's no search terms report and no placement report.


- Custom audience lists need at least 25,000 matched users, which rules out most independent merchants. And you get exactly one ad format, a text ad with a small thumbnail.


Someone who spends their days buying ads[had a pretty telling take on r/PPC:](https://www.reddit.com/r/PPC/comments/1w7xyea/anybody_positive_experience_with_chatgpt_ads/)


> *“Conversion performance is well below Google, Meta, or MS at this point for most advertisers. But the platform will very likely improve; keep in mind that we've only had conversion tracking since June and performance based bidding for weeks.”*


So, judging the platform on today's numbers is a bit like judging Facebook ads in 2009. But still, just for the sake of it, here’s a comparison table of how ChatGPT ads compare to other platforms that you might already be using:


Table Factors ChatGPT Ads Google Search Meta Amazon Ads SEO/AEO


What you buy A sponsored block below the answer A slot above the results Attention inside a feed A slot in shopping results and on product pages Nothing, you earn it


Targeting Context hints, no keywords Keywords and audiences Interests, lookalikes, behavior Keywords, products, categories Whatever the query matches


Typical CPC $3 to $5 Around $2 $0.78 $0.85 to $1.30 for Sponsored Products $0, paid in time instead

## So, should you be marketing on ChatGPT?


It is worth testing now if you:


- Sell physical products to price-conscious consumers.


- Already see ChatGPT showing up as a referral source in your analytics.


- Sell something people research before buying, like furniture, appliances, electronics, bikes, tools, or anything below roughly $100.


- Have a few hundred dollars you would be genuinely relaxed about losing while you learn the platform.


- Can install a pixel and read GA4 without hiring someone, since the platform's own reporting won't tell you much.


### If you want to test it, follow these steps


1. Give yourself four weeks and a budget you'd be relaxed about losing, somewhere around $500.


1. Install the pixel before you spend a dollar, because retroactive attribution does not exist and you'll be left arguing with yourself about whether it worked.


1. Tag every ad with unique UTM parameters so your analytics can tell you what that traffic did after it landed, since the platform's own reporting won't.


1. Build several ad groups with different context hints rather than one broad campaign, then look at engagement time and conversion rate per group instead of running after click-through rate, which tells you almost nothing here.


1. Then compare it against your existing channels. If it loses on cost per acquisition but brings in genuinely new customers who were mid-research, that might still be worth something to you.


That being said, the harder problem shows up after the click. A stranger who found you through an AI recommendation has no history with your brand, so every doubt they would normally park for a trusted store gets asked at checkout instead.


## So if you are worrying about trust...


There’s a way you can show your customers that you care about them, especially when you acquire them through ChatGPT ads.


Adding a warranty to your checkout or post-purchase strategy can work as a[signal of trust.](https://www.surebright.com/blog/trust-recession-in-ecommerce-why-building-trust-with-customers-is-harder-than-ever) Protection coverage works better than another badge or another discount code. Rather than giving them the reason to think you are upselling, it helps your customer build peace of mind for a product they’ve already purchased. That’s just what many renowned brands did –[Sennheiser reduced return rates](https://www.surebright.com/blog/sennheisers-growth-playbook-cementing-a-built-to-last-reputation-in-the-age-of-disposable-tech) through warranty integrations and got high attach rates in return.
